title: Delete a branch on the server (and put it back)
summary: Local and remote branches are separate things. Delete one on the server, see what that does and does not affect, then restore it from a clone that still has it.
mental_model: `git push origin --delete x` means 'push nothing to the ref named x', which deletes it. The old spelling `git push origin :x` says the same thing literally: empty source, destination x.
danger: Deleting a branch on a server that has no other copy can strand its commits. On GitHub they are recoverable for a while; on a bare repo you control, they are gone once garbage collection runs.

commit.message: Draft that should not have been pushed

steps.title: See what exists where
steps.why: Three branches on the server, three locally, and a teammate clone that also has one of them. Deletion affects exactly one of these copies at a time.

steps.title: Delete the merged branch on the server
steps.why: `--delete` removes the branch from origin. Your local branch still exists — the two are separate refs joined only by tracking config.
steps.expect: Gone from origin, still present locally.

verify.label: the branch is gone from the server

steps.title: Clean up your local copy too
steps.why: `-d` accepts it because the work is merged into main. Deleting the remote branch never deletes your local one; you always do both.

verify.label: the local branch is cleaned up too

steps.title: Delete the draft that should not be public
steps.why: Same command, different motive. Note what it does NOT do: the commit is still in the server's object database until it is garbage-collected, and it is still in the teammate's clone.

verify.label: the draft branch is gone from the server

steps.title: Prove deletion is not erasure
steps.why: The teammate's clone still has the branch and every commit on it. This is the crucial point about anything sensitive: deleting a remote branch is not a security measure — it is tidying.
steps.expect: The draft, still fully readable in the clone.

steps.title: Restore the branch from that clone
steps.why: Any clone holding the commits can push the branch back. This is the recovery route when someone deletes a branch that was not finished — no server-side undo required.

verify.label: the branch is back on the server
verify.hint: push it from any clone that still has the commits

steps.title: Update your own view
steps.why: Your clone knows nothing about the restoration until you fetch. Deleting, restoring and pruning all operate on different copies — which is the entire lesson of this scenario.

verify.label: your clone sees the restored branch after a fetch
the merged branch was deleted on the server
and locally too — they are two separate deletions
the draft branch was restored from a clone that still had it
verify.hint: push it back from the teammate clone, then fetch

verify.label: the restored branch has its original content

pitfalls: `git branch -d` deletes locally only. `git push origin --delete` deletes remotely only. Nothing does both, and forgetting the second is why servers accumulate hundreds of branches.
Deleting a branch containing a leaked secret does not remove the secret. The commit stays in the object database, in every clone, and in any CI cache. Rotate the credential.
The old `git push origin :branch` syntax still works and appears in older documentation. It is the same operation.
If the server has branch protection, deletion is refused — which is a feature, not a bug, on main.
